rationale: A wins because it knows the difference between an angle and a decoration. Its best line, "Peloton's churn just hit a record low. Nobody's said why yet," turns a real fact into a sharp reporting question without pretending causality. B has useful bones, but "The Target Customer Is Not Who Bought One in 2020" and "More Loyal Subscribers Than Ever" smuggle in unsupported narrative sugar. That's how a decent pitch gets cavities.
gaps_in_A: "Peloton's next act: renting bikes instead of selling them" overstates the shift; the update says Peloton is expanding rental nationwide, not replacing sales.

"Peloton is calling itself profitable" is a little too cute unless the company literally used that wording; the supplied facts say positive adjusted EBITDA and free cash flow, while net income remains negative.
The CEO angle needs the CEO's name before it can become a real pitch; A flags this, but the headline still leans on an unnamed protagonist.
gaps_in_B: "What Did He Actually Slash?" invents gender for the new CEO. Small word, real credibility leak.
"The Target Customer Is Not Who Bought One in 2020" is not in the update. No 2020 buyer profile, no target-customer data, no evidence of a demographic shift.
"Three Years After Its Pandemic Crash" and "companies that became symbols of pandemic excess" import outside narrative without evidence from the supplied update.
"What Keeps 6 Million Peloton Subscribers Paying" confuses total members with subscribers; the update says total members exceed 6 million, not that 6 million subscribers are paying.
